hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Bananas contain unusually high levels of polyphenol oxidase, or PPO, an enzyme responsible for browning that also degrades polyphenols. 

That's why, on the occasion I happen to make a smoothie, I usually use a lower-PPO ingredient such as avocado instead.

A high-PPO banana smoothie reduced peak blood levels of epicatechin-derived metabolites by 84% in a small, crossover experiment. A low-PPO mixed-berry smoothie preserved exposure.

This was primarily a cocoa-epicatechin experiment rather than a direct test of blueberry anthocyanins or health outcomes. But PPO can oxidize epicatechin and blueberry chlorogenic acid, and the resulting compounds indirectly degrade anthocyanins.

Bananas are healthy. But I think leaving them out of a food combination where they can interact too directly with polyphenols is a sensible optimization.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick notes bananas are high in an enzyme (PPO) that can knock down polyphenols in a smoothie. In one small trial, a banana smoothie cut peak epicatechin metabolites by about 84% versus a berry mix.

Bananas are still fine food. The tip is about mixing: if you're chasing berries or cocoa for the plant compounds, don't blend them with banana every time.

Have the banana on the side, or blend berries with yoghurt or avocado instead.
hits.video_tip: 15–20s kitchen bench; banana next to a berry bowl; captions “Banana’s fine.” then “Don’t blend it with your berries every time.”

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Two days of a high-dose oat diet lowered LDL cholesterol by 10% in adults with metabolic syndrome.

Participants ate 300 grams of rolled oats per day (about 4 cups). By contrast, eating 80 grams daily for six weeks did not significantly lower cholesterol.

What I find especially interesting is the mechanism. Oats shifted the gut microbiome and increased phenolic metabolites, including dihydroferulic acid. These changes tracked with the cholesterol reduction.

Oat beta-glucan is already known to lower LDL. These microbial metabolites may be another piece of the puzzle, and another reason I eat whole oats once or twice a week.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick shared a study: two days of a high-dose oat diet (300 g of rolled oats a day, about 4 cups) cut LDL cholesterol by 10% in adults with metabolic syndrome. A smaller 80 g a day for six weeks didn't do much.

That's a lot of oats. It was a short, heavy trial, not a daily rule.

Still, plain rolled oats are cheap, filling fuel before a shift. If your cholesterol's up, ask your GP whether more oats and fibre are worth a go.
hits.video_tip: 15s kitchen bench with a bag of rolled oats and a measuring cup; captions “300 g of oats, 2 days.” then “LDL down 10%.”

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text:
High LDL but Low Blood Pressure 🩸

One reason I might have no detectable soft or calcified coronary plaque (0 mm3), despite my historically astronomical LDL cholesterol (PMID: 42187880), is my low blood pressure.

Here's a bit of biology: Atherosclerosis isn't simply about LDL…
hits.draft_en:
Nick Norwitz says one reason he may have zero plaque in his heart arteries despite very high LDL is his low blood pressure. Artery damage isn't only about LDL.

That's not a reason to ignore cholesterol. It's a reminder that blood pressure counts too.

Get your blood pressure checked (a lot of chemists will do it for free) and know your numbers, not just your cholesterol.
hits.video_tip: 15s face-to-cam next to a blood-pressure cuff; captions “It’s not just LDL.” then “Know your blood pressure.”

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
"Who will dare to write a history of human goodness?"

Even though my professional world is filled with a focus on metabolic health, my personal reading often focuses on history, economics, civilization, and religion. Will Durant, a historian who spans all of those topics, posed that question above in The Lessons of History. I keep thinking about it. 

I think there are two reasons a history of human goodness has never been written. First, goodness isn't sensational. Historians record wars and scandals because they're exceptional, and today's social media algorithms reward outrage for the same reason. Second, most of the good that people do is never known at all, because the people doing it don't want the credit.

But kindness really is common. And commonly overlooked. Most people, on most days, are good to the people around them.
